claims.claim: OPERAM enrolled 2,008 adults aged 70 or over with multimorbidity and polypharmacy admitted to university hospitals in four European countries; a doctor and pharmacist used STOPP/START software to review medicines; the main outcome was a first drug-related readmission within 12 months.
claims.supporting_passage: "110 clusters of inpatient wards within university based hospitals in four European countries (Switzerland, Netherlands, Belgium, and Republic of Ireland) defined by attending hospital doctors." "2008 older adults (≥70 years) with multimorbidity (≥3 chronic conditions) and polypharmacy (≥5 drugs used long term)." "Clinical staff clusters were randomised to usual care or a structured pharmacotherapy optimisation intervention performed at the individual level jointly by a doctor and a pharmacist, with the support of a clinical decision software system deploying the screening tool of older person's prescriptions and screening tool to alert to the right treatment (STOPP/START) criteria to identify potentially inappropriate prescribing." "Primary outcome was first drug related hospital admission within 12 months."
claims.location: Abstract (Setting, Participants, Interventions, Main outcome measures)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 70+, 3+ chronic conditions, 5+ long-term drugs, hospital inpatients (medical and surgical), Switzerland/Netherlands/Belgium/Ireland; single in-hospital structured review with STOPP/START software plus GP letter vs usual care; first adjudicated drug-related readmission; 12 months
claims.safe_wording: A European trial of 2,008 people aged 70 or over, each with at least 3 long-term conditions and at least 5 regular medicines, tested a structured medicines review in hospital, done by a doctor and a pharmacist with the help of checklist software (STOPP/START). The main question was whether it reduced readmissions caused by medicines over the next year.
claims.qualifications: Hospital inpatients in university hospitals; the review happened once, during the admission, with recommendations also sent to the GP.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None for the design description.

Table 5 (Control n, events (%); Intervention n, events (%); odds ratio (95% CI); P): "Drug misuse§:  2  893  378 (42.3)  832  355 (42.7)  0.99 (0.81 to 1.20)  0.92  Drug overuse§:  2  893  376 (42.1)  832  348 (41.8)  0.99 (0.82 to 1.20)  0.91  Drug underuse§:  2  893  638 (71.4)  832  583 (70.1)  0.91 (0.70 to 1.17)  0.45  Mean (SD) No of long term drugs¶:  2  893  11.0 (4.27)  833  11.2 (4.54)  −0.13 (−0.49 to 0.22)  0.47". Results: "Drug related outcomes, pain, activities of daily living status, and drug adherence did not differ significantly between the groups, except for quality of life at 12 months, which was better in the intervention group (between group adjusted mean difference 2.29, 95% confidence interval 0.31 to 4.26,)." "Among attending clinicians in the intervention group, implementation of SENATOR software-generated medication advice points was poor (~15%)." STOPP/START v3 Discussion: "Recent analysis of the specific STOPP and START criteria elicited in the OPERAM trial shows that over half of all the STOPP and START recommendations generated by the software tool were not  considered clinically relevant in individual cases []."
claims.location: SENATOR Abstract (Results); STOPP/START v3 full text, Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: SENATOR: 1537 older inpatients, six European centres, ADRs within 14 days of randomisation. OPERAM relevance analysis: reported second-hand in the v3 paper
claims.safe_wording: In a second European trial (SENATOR), hospital doctors acted on only about 15 in 100 of the software's suggestions, and side effects in hospital were no less common (about 25 in 100 in both groups).
claims.qualifications: The OPERAM relevance finding is reported second-hand in the STOPP/START v3 paper; the original analysis was not opened, so quote it only as 'a later analysis reported'. SENATOR has a corrigendum whose content was not opened.

"START criteria are designed to detect potential prescribing omissions (PPOs) which represent another critically important aspect of inappropriate prescribing, i.e., undertreatment or failure to prescribe appropriate medications despite clear and valid indications." "Over the course of four rounds of Delphi validation, the panel achieved consensus on 133 STOPP criteria and 57 START criteria, i.e., 190 STOPP/START criteria in total" "These criteria cannot replace clinical judgment in individual cases"
claims.location: Full text, Background; Abstract (Results); Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Explicit criteria for older people with multimorbidity and polypharmacy; European expert consensus (11 geriatricians, 8 countries)
claims.safe_wording: The main European checklist for medicines in older people has two halves: one lists medicines to consider stopping, the other lists medicines that may be missing. The 2023 version has 133 items of the first kind and 57 of the second.
claims.qualifications: Consensus criteria; the authors say they cannot replace clinical judgement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

"The updated criteria continue to focus on situations that require caution in multimorbid older people, such as the prescribing of anticoagulants in patients with chronic atrial fibrillation and concurrent increased risk of bleeding (c.f. claims.claim: Potential prescribing omissions are about as common as potentially inappropriate medicines: in 25,854 Dutch primary care patients aged 65 or over, 74.3% had at least one omission and 72.2% at least one potentially inappropriate medicine over 6 years; the most common omission was a laxative for someone on regular opioids.
claims.supporting_passage: "All 25,854 patients aged 65 years and older having at least 5 contacts with their practice in 6 years were included." "In our population, 72.2% and 74.3% of patients had at least 1 PIM and PPO, respectively; 30.9% and 34.2% had at least 3 PIMs and PPOs, respectively." Full-text excerpt: "the most frequently observed PPO was "start laxatives in patients receiving opioids regularly" (14.7% of all PPOs)."

claims.safe_wording: In a Dutch study of almost 26,000 people aged 65 or over, about 3 in 4 were missing at least one medicine the checklist says may be indicated at some point over 6 years; a similar share had at least one medicine it says may be inappropriate. The most common gap was a laxative for someone on a regular opioid.

"Polypharmacy was present in 61% of 150 patients. Underprescription was found in 47 (31%). Of patients with polypharmacy 42.9% were undertreated, in contrast to 13.5% of patients using four medicines or less (OR 4.8, 95% CI 2.0, 11.2). The estimated probability of underprescription increased significantly with the number of drugs."

claims.claim: A medication review judged by the number of medicines removed will miss omissions.
claims.supporting_passage: No source states this directly. Supporting facts: omissions are as common as potentially inappropriate medicines (te Winkel: "72.2% and 74.3% of patients had at least 1 PIM and PPO, respectively"); STOPP/START is designed for "deprescribing of adverse medication and introduction of beneficial medication (where inappropriately unprescribed)".

claims.qualifications: This is a judgement; present it as the post's position ('we should'), not as a finding. No study found here measured whether reviews targeted at reducing counts miss omissions.

candidates.reason: The judge's concern is confirmed. OPERAM's randomised comparison did not show a clear between-group reduction in inappropriate prescribing: at 2 months drug overuse was 41.8% vs 42.1% (OR 0.99) and underuse 70.1% vs 71.4%, and number of long-term drugs was about 11 in both arms. The abstract's 'was reduced' refers to recommendations implemented within the intervention arm. So the opening 'cut inappropriate prescribing' is not supported. The 62.2% figure has a denominator of the 789 with a recommendation, not all intervention participants. The readmission result (21.9% vs 22.4%, HR 0.95, 0.77 to 1.17) and the rest of the chain are supported, and SENATOR (about 15% implemented) and Cochrane 2023 support the wider reading.
candidates.revised_angle: Read a medicines-review trial step by step. In OPERAM (2,008 people aged 70 or over, four European countries), the review flagged something for 86 in 100 people who received it; for about 6 in 10 of those, at least one change was made by 2 months. But at 2 months about 42 in 100 people in both groups were still on a medicine judged overused, and over the next year about 22 in 100 in each group were readmitted because of a medicine. Each step can lose the effect. Test for the next trial: did it show a difference from the control group at each step, and did it measure an outcome patients value? Opening suggestion: 'A European trial found a problem with the medicines of 86 in 100 older people it reviewed. Two months later, the control group's medicines looked much the same as theirs.' Do not say the trial cut or reduced inappropriate prescribing.

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported from the full text of the PRIME incidence paper and the abstract plus full-text excerpts of the prediction paper: 413 of 1,116 (37%) had medication-related harm within 8 weeks (mostly side effects; 40% rated only 'possible'); 328 of 413 used NHS care for it (about 29 in 100 of all followed up) and 87 were readmitted (about 8 in 100); doctors' predictions showed no relationship with harm (OR 1.10, 0.82 to 1.46). The judge's concerns are handled by wording: explain what counted as harm, and do not say 'whatever their experience' because only 126 predictions came from senior doctors. The confidence result (OR 1.58) goes the other way and should be stated. The call for routine follow-up (for example a community pharmacy check) is a judgement: effectiveness of routine follow-up is not established and no specific NHS service was verified in this batch.

Duncan 2019 full text supports the core claims: in 2017 interviews, 13 GPs and 10 pharmacists said most reviews were done remotely without the patient because of workload, several called them a 'tick box' exercise, and stopping medicines was harder because it required involving the patient. The limitation (23 professionals from trial practices, no patients, no frequency data) is explicit in the paper and must be stated. NICE's emphasis on involving the person is supported by Duncan's peer-reviewed description plus a NICE search extract (page not opened), so phrase it generally. Because the interviews predate England's structured medication reviews (September 2020), the post must date the evidence; a 2025 survey of 120 SMR pharmacists found most reviews by phone and only 26% giving information in advance. 'You can ask' is a suggestion, not a verified entitlement. Do not claim the record literally shows 'review done'; label the visual illustrative.

Reeve 2018 supports 92.0% (1752 of 1981, weighted) willing to stop one or more regular medicines if their doctor said it was possible, and 66.6% wanting fewer medicines. The prescriber-reluctance premise now has a primary UK source (Duncan 2019 interviews), not just Reeve's introduction. Chock 2021 (29 studies, 11,049 participants) gives a consistent pooled 87.6% and notes that attitude tools predict behaviour poorly. The conditional ('if my doctor said it was possible') should be the point, as the judge advised. The adjusted OR for 6+ medicines is optional, must not be converted, and conflicts with the meta-analysis. Reserve.

The core argument is supported: STOPP/START covers omissions as well as excess (v3 full text), omissions are about as common as inappropriate medicines (74.3% vs 72.2% over 6 years in 25,854 Dutch patients), the most common omission there was a laxative with regular opioids, and underprescribing is linked with polypharmacy (Kuijpers). But the intended claim that START version 3 includes 'laxative with regular opioids' is not verified: the v3 criteria appendix could not be opened, and a v3 study lists 'regular opioids without concomitant laxatives' among potentially inappropriate medicines (STOPP side). The AF anticoagulation example is supported from the v3 main text but must carry the bleeding-risk caution and 'when indicated and wanted'. The King's Fund distinction is supported only second-hand. 'A review judged by drugs removed will miss omissions' is a judgement. Reserve.
candidates.revised_angle: Open with the laxative example worded as 'the European STOPP/START checklist flags a regular opioid painkiller taken without a laxative' (no version or START label). Then: in a Dutch study of almost 26,000 people aged 65 or over, about 3 in 4 had at least one possibly missing medicine over 6 years, as many as had a possibly unnecessary one, and the commonest gap was that laxative. Second example: an anticoagulant for untreated persistent atrial fibrillation, when the person wants it and bleeding risk allows (the same checklist flags bleeding caution). Close with the judgement, marked as such: a review should be judged by how well the medicines fit the person, not by how many are stopped. Avoid bone-protection examples (E095, E097).
